start.text: Still here. So are they, now.
He came up. Took him long enough. Took me longer.

first.text: An old woman sits on a coil of hawser by the lane-house door, under the lashed horn, in a guild coat buttoned to the chin and a white shawl crossed over it. Her hand rests on the horn's frame as if it might get up and go without her.
Long, and two short. That's Oda Farrow's horn; she always did hurry the shorts. I heard it. I heard both.
Wenna Garrow. Lane-warden. I swore that girl master in this house thirty-eight years back, and she cried, and I'll thank you not to tell her I said so.

why.text: A horn answered is a lane promised. That's the oldest law we've got. You answer a boat when you can light her in, and not before.
The Wrack's dark. The Teeth are out there in the fog where they've always been, and nobody can see them. So nobody answers.
She looks at the lashed horn. The tarred line round its mouthpiece is wound thick, the way you'd bind a wound.
I answered once. The night the Spire went dark.

gannet.text: The Gannet blew for us at dusk, coming home from salvage off the Teeth. Long and two short. I answered, as I'd answered fifty years. And while my note was still in the air, the Wrack went out.
She came in on my answer. The Teeth had her. Three aboard.
We hauled her up on the hard. The yard keeps what the sea gives back; that's the law too. Jory's down there now, taking off her copper.
And I can't tell you their names. That's the fog: it takes the names first. Three of ours, and I swore every one, and I can't say who.
Every Tidewright boat carries her crew chalked on a board at the stern. The Gannet's has gone blank as a slate. Oda says you carry a light that gives things back.
...You've looked already. I can see it on you.
Hold it to the board. I'd say their names over the horn. It's the least a warden owes, and it's all I've left to pay with.

choice.text: The Gannet's crew: Hale Corbet, master. Annis Corbet. Ruan Pask.
What would it take to light the Wrack?
I've been out to the Wrack.
Oda says Tidewrights weigh a deed.
Thornwold's beacon-keeper has lost its name.

names.text: Wenna takes her hand off the frame and lays it flat on the horn, over the lashing, where a mouth would go.
Hale Corbet. Master. Annis Corbet, his girl. Ruan Pask.

She doesn't sound the horn. She says each name into the bound mouth of it, low, the way you'd tell somebody a thing in their sleep. The third time round, the lane-house shutters open a crack, and somebody inside says them too.
There. They're home. That's what a horn's for, in the end: saying who's come in.
And I'll say the rest, since you've earned it. It was my answer brought them in. Not the dark. Not the Keepers. Mine.
Jory thinks it was the Keepers' dark that drowned his brother, and I've let him. It's easier to hate a light that went out than an old woman who's still sitting here.
I'll not ask you to lie for me. I'll not ask you to tell him, either. I'm done asking things of people.

wrack.text: Light it. That's all. It'll want feeding, same as your others, Oda says: something somebody holds.
It stands on its stack out on the Teeth. At the bottom of a spring tide the Teeth come up out of the water enough to walk, if you know where to put your feet. I knew, once.
Ask me again when the tide's down. It isn't.

teeth.text: I've sat here since you went off trying to remember where to put my feet. And I've remembered I never knew. Nobody did.

You put them on the white. Every spring, at the bottom of the springs, the lampwardens went out with a pot of white lead and put a hand on every rock that would bear you. Hale Corbet did it, these last years. You didn't learn the Teeth; you learned to look for the white.

You put them on the white. Every spring, at the bottom of the springs, the lampwardens went out with a pot of white lead and put a hand on every rock that would bear you. The Gannet's master did it, these last years, and I can't give you his name. You didn't learn the Teeth; you learned to look for the white.
The fog'll have had them off, same as it had the Gannet's board. But you've a light that gives things back.
And tonight's the bottom of the springs, near enough. Go out to the end of the spit and wait it down. Come back before the flood. It doesn't wait for anybody, and it won't wait for you.

deed.text: We do. Oda weighed you on her scale at Saltmarrow, and she's told me what it came to, and what it's come to since. Three lit.
She says you told it like a thing you'd done. Good. A deed ought to be owned.
She says you told it as if half of it was other people's. That's the Tidewright way, near enough.
She says you'd not tell it at all. That's allowed. The scale doesn't need telling.
Keepers want the Spire lit their way, by their rites, with their hands on it. We don't care whose hands. We only want to steer by it.
When the Wrack's lit, come into the lane-house, and I'll swear you a friend of the lanes. No Tidewright deck would ever weigh you light again. Think on it. It's not nothing, from us.

sleeve.text: Wenna looks at the faded ember on its scrap of robe without touching it.
Oda told me before you were off her plank. It's ridden four lanes on her deck and paid its way, she says. I'll take her word. It's what she's for.
You never showed Oda that, I'd wager. No. She'd have told me.
Keepers pay twice on our decks. You'll have heard. Once for the crossing, like anybody. And once into the Book.

Every Keeper that ever rode a Tidewright deck wrote their name in the lane-house Book, for the second fare. The one thing a Keeper won't give anybody else, they gave us. Nine hundred years of them, in the dark at the back of the house.
Put it away before Jory sees it. He's got enough to carry.

book.text: Thirty winters at Thornwold's light, and it's lost its own name? Hm.
Keepers pay twice on our decks: once for the crossing, and once into the Book. Their names, in the lane-house Book, in their own hands. It's the one thing a Keeper won't give anybody else.
If your Keeper ever rode a Tidewright deck out to Thornwold, it wrote its name in the Book first. Thirty winters back. It'll be in there.
The Book's at the back of the house. I'll not take a lamp in there till the Wrack's lit: ordinary fire's no use against this fog, and the Book's paper. Light the Wrack, and I'll find you its page.

marks.text: Out at the spit's end, and wait it down. The white's there or it isn't.
It'll be there. Hale never missed a spring.

wrack_seen.text: You've been up. I can see it on you: you've the look of somebody who's read a lot of names.

Aye, that's where they go. A year and a tide, and if nobody comes for her, a boat goes out to the Wrack, a timber at a time, and holds the light up for the rest. It's what we owe them. It's what they owe us.
The new bracket's for the Gannet. Hale fitted it himself, the spring before. He liked a thing ready.
The new bracket's for the Gannet. Her master fitted it himself, the spring before. He liked a thing ready.
So it wants feeding. Something somebody holds. I'll sit with that a while.
So it wants feeding. Something somebody holds. The lad and I will sit with that a while.
